readings.c1s1:
¶
'''witchingly''' (wich′ing-li), ''adv.'' In a bewitching, fascinating, or enchanting manner. ''Thomson'', Castle of Indolence, i. 6.

'''witch-knot''' (wich′not), ''n.'' A knot or snarl, especially in the hair, supposed to be caused by witchcraft. Compare ''elf'', ''v.'', and ''elf-lock.''
{{smaller block|<poem>O, that I were a witch but for her sake!
Yfaith her Queenship little rest should take;
I’d scratch that face, that may not feele the aire,
And knit whole ropes of ''witch-knots'' in her haire.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Poems (ed. 1637), p. 253. (''Halliwell.'')}}
<poem>O wha has loosed the nine ''witch-knots''
That were amang that ladye’s locks?</poem>
{{right|''Willie’s Ladye'' (Child’s Ballads, I. 166).}}}}

'''witch-meal''' (wich′mēl), ''n.'' The powdery pollen of the club-moss, ''Lycopodium clavatum''; lycopode. It is so rapidly inflammable as to have been used in theaters to represent lightning.

'''witch-ridden''' (wich′rid″n), ''a.'' Ridden by witches; having a nightmare.

'''witch-seeker''' (wich′sē″kėr), ''n.'' Same as ''witch-finder.''

'''witch-stitch''' (wich′stich), ''n.'' In ''embroidery'', same as ''herring-bone stitch'' (which see, under ''herring-bone'').

'''witchuck''' (wich′uk), ''n.'' Same as ''witch-chick.''

'''witch-wife''' (wich′wīf), ''n.'' A woman who practises witchcraft.
{{smaller block|In the tenth century we hear of the first instance of a death in England for heresy, in the actual drowning of a ''witch-wife'' at London Bridge.
{{right|''J. R. Green'', Conq. of Eng., p. 11.}}}}

'''witch-wolf†''' (wich′wu̇lf), ''n.'' A werwolf. ''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, II. 119.

¶
'''witch-wood''' (wich′wu̇d), ''n.'' '''1.''' Same as ''witchen.'' —'''2.''' Same as ''witch-elm.''—'''3.''' The spindle-tree, ''Euonymus Europæus.''

'''wit-cracker†''' (wit′krak″ėr), ''n.'' One who makes jests; a joker.
{{smaller block|A college of ''wit-crackers'' cannot flout me out of my humour: Dost thou think I care for a satire, or an epigram?
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, v. 4. 102.}}}}

'''wit-craft†''' (wit′krȧft), ''n.'' '''1.''' Mental skill; contrivance; invention. ''Camden'', Remains, p. 144. (''Nares.'')—'''2.''' The art of reasoning; logic.
{{smaller block|Master Secretary Wilson, geuing an English name to his arte of Logicke, called it ''Witcraft.''
{{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 191.}}}}

'''wite<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''witen'', < AS. ''wītan'', see: see ''wit''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''wite''<sup>2</sup>.] To observe; keep; guard; preserve; protect.
{{smaller block|“Pieres,” quod I, “I preye the whi stonde thise piles here?”
“For wyndes, wiltow wyte,” quod he, “to ''witen'' it fram fallynge.”
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xvi. 25.}}}}

'''wite<sup>2</sup>''' (wīt), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''witen'', ''wyten'', < AS. ''wītan'', ''wītian'', impute, blame, censure, punish, fine (cf. ''wītnian'', punish, ''edwītan'', reproach, ''ætwītan'', reproach: see ''twit''), = Icel. ''vīta'', fine, = Goth. ''weitjan'' (in ''idweitjan'', reproach (= AS. ''edwītan''), and in ''fair-weitjan'', observe intently); ult. connected with ''wītan'', see, ''witan'', know: see ''wite''<sup>1</sup>, ''wit''<sup>1</sup>, and cf. ''twit''.] '''1†.''' To impute (to one) as a fault; blame for; blame (that): governing directly a noun or clause, and taking an indirect object in the dative.
{{smaller block|<poem>And therfore, if that I mysspeke or seye,
''Wyte'' it the ale of Southwerk, I yow preye.</poem>}}

{{smaller block|In the tenth century we hear of the first instance of a death in England for heresy, in the actual drowning of a ''witch-wife'' at London Bridge.
{{right|''J. R. Green'', Conq. of Eng., p. 11.}}}}

'''witch-wolf†''' (wich′wu̇lf), ''n.'' A werwolf.   ''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, II. 119.

'''witch-wood''' (wich′wu̇d), ''n.'' '''1.''' Same as ''witchen.'' —'''2.''' Same as ''witch-elm.''—'''3.''' The spindle-tree, ''Euonymus Europæus.''

'''wit-cracker†''' (wit′krak″ėr), ''n.'' One who makes jests; a joker.
{{smaller block|A college of ''wit-crackers'' cannot flout me out of my humour: Dost thou think I care for a satire, or an epigram?
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, v. 4. 102.}}}}

'''wit-craft†''' (wit′krȧft), ''n.'' '''1.''' Mental skill; contrivance; invention.   ''Camden'', Remains, p. 144. (''Nares.'')—'''2.''' The art of reasoning; logic.
{{smaller block|Master Secretary Wilson, geuing an English name to his arte of Logicke, called it ''Witcraft.''
{{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 191.}}}}

'''wite<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v. t.''   [ME. ''witen'', < AS. ''wītan'', see: see ''wit''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''wite''<sup>2</sup>.]   To observe; keep; guard; preserve; protect.
{{smaller block|“Pieres,” quod I, “I preye the whi stonde thise piles here?”
“For wyndes, wiltow wyte,” quod he, “to ''witen'' it fram fallynge.”
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xvi. 25.}}}}

'''wite<sup>2</sup>''' (wīt), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''witen'', ''wyten'', < AS. ''wītan'', ''wītian'', impute, blame, censure, punish, fine (cf. ''wītnian'', punish, ''edwītan'', reproach, ''ætwītan'', reproach: see ''twit''), = Icel. ''vīta'', fine, = Goth. ''weitjan'' (in ''idweitjan'', reproach (= AS. ''edwītan''), and in ''fair-weitjan'', observe intently); ult. connected with ''wītan'', see, ''witan'', know: see ''wite''<sup>1</sup>, ''wit''<sup>1</sup>, and cf. ''twit''.]   '''1†.''' To impute (to one) as a fault; blame for; blame (that): governing directly a noun or clause, and taking an indirect object in the dative.
{{smaller block|<poem>And therfore, if that I mysspeke or seye,
''Wyte'' it the ale of Southwerk, I yow preye.</poem> {{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Miller’s Tale, l. 33.}}}}
{{smaller block|Y pray yow . . . not to ''wyte'' it me that y am the causer of it that my seyd maister noyeth yow with so manye materes. {{right|''Paston Letters'', I. 374.}}}}
'''2.''' To impute wrong to; find fault with; blame; censure. [Now Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>He gan fowly ''wyte''
His wicked fortune. ''Spenser'', F. Q., III. iv. 52.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>O ''wyte'' na me, now, my master dear,
I garr’d a’ my young hawks sing.</poem>{{right|''Lord John'' (Child’s Ballads, I. 136).}}}}

'''wite'''<sup>2</sup> (wīt), ''n.''   [Formerly also ''wight''; < ME. ''wite'', ''wyte'', < AS. ''wīte'', punishment, fine, torment, torture, = OS. ''wīti'' = OHG. ''wīzi'', MHG. ''wīze'', punishment, = Icel. ''víti'', fine: see ''wite''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' Blame; censure; reproach; fault. [Now Scotch.]
{{smaller block|For worche he wel other wrong, the ''wit'' is his oune. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (A), x. 75.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And but I do, sirs, lat me han the ''wyte''.</poem>{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Canon’s Yeoman’s Tale, l. 400.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>“Put na the ''wite'' on me,” she said,
“It was my may Catherine.”</poem>{{right|''Earl Richard'' (Child’s Ballads, III. 8).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>They hae kill’d Sir Charlie Hay,
And they laid the ''wyte'' on Geordie.</poem>{{right|''Geordie'' (Child’s Ballads, VIII. 93).}}}}
'''2.''' Punishment; penalty; mulct; fine; in ''old Eng. criminal law'', a fine paid to the king or other lord in respect of an offense.   ''J. F. Stephen.''

'''wite<sup>3</sup>†''', ''v. i.''   [ME. ''witen''; < AS. ''wītan'' (pret. ''wāt''), ''gewitan'' (pret. ''gewāt''), go.]   To go.
{{smaller block|Ne ''wite'' thow noght fra me.
{{right|''Early Eng. Psalter'' (ed. Stevenson), xxi. 12.}}}}

'''wite<sup>4</sup>†''', ''v.'' and ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''wit''<sup>1</sup>.

'''witeless†''' (wīt′les), ''a.''   [< ''wite''<sup>2</sup> + ''-less''.]   Blameless.
{{smaller block|Ne can Willye wite the ''witelesse'' herdgroome.
{{right|''Spenser'', Shep. Cal., August.}}}}

'''witenagemot''' (wit′e-nạ-ge-mōt′), ''n.''   [AS. ''witena gemōt'', ‘counselors’ moot’: ''witena'', gen. pl. of ''wita'', ''weota'', ''gewita'', a man of knowledge, a counselor; ''gemōt'', moot or meet, assembly, council, parliament: see ''wit''<sup>2</sup> and ''moot''<sup>1</sup>.]   In ''Anglo-Saxon hist.'', the great national council or parliament, consisting of the king with his dependents and friends and sometimes the members of his family, the ealdormen, the bishops, and other ecclesiastics. {{smaller|This council, which met frequently, constituted the highest court of judicature in the kingdom. It was summoned by the king in any political emergency, and its concurrence was necessary in many important measures, such as the deciding of war, the levying of extraordinary taxes, grants of land in certain cases, election and (in many instances) deposition of kings.}}
{{smaller block|The old Germanic tradition, which associated “the wise men” in all royal action, gave a constitutional ground to the powers which the ''Witenagemot'' exercised more and more as English society took a more and more aristocratic form; and it thus came to share with the crown in the higher justice, in the imposition of taxes, the making of laws, the conclusion of treaties, the control of war, the disposal of public lands, the appointment of bishops and great officers of state. There were times when it claimed even to elect or depose a king.
{{right|''J. R. Green'', Conq. of Eng., p. 216.}}}}

'''witerliche†, witerli†''', ''adv.'' See ''witterly.''

'''witfish''' (wit′fish), ''n.'' Same as ''whitefish.''

'''witful†''' (wit′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ME. ''witful, witfol, witvol;'' < ''wit''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ful.'']   Full of wit, knowledge, or wisdom; wise; knowing; sensible.
{{smaller block|Tis passing miraculous that your dul and blind worship should so sodainly turne both sightfull and ''witfull.''
{{right|''Chapman,'' Masque of Middle Temple and Lincoln’s Inn.}}}}

'''with'''<sup>1</sup> (wiᴛ̵ʜ), ''prep.''   [< ME. ''with,'' rarely ''wit, wid,'' with, near, among, in company with, also against, along, on, to, from, by, < AS. ''with,'' against, opposite, = OS. ''widh'' = OFries. ''with'' = Icel. ''vith,'' against, by, at, with, = Sw. ''vid,'' near, at, by, = Dan. ''ved,'' by, at; otherwise in the compar. form ''wither-,'' AS. ''wither-'' = OHG. ''widar,'' MHG. G. ''wider,'' against, ''wieder,'' again, = Goth. ''withra,'' against, toward, in front of; cf. Skt. ''vitaram,'' further, ''vi-,'' asunder, L. ''ve-,'' apart. Cf. ''with-, wither''<sup>1</sup>, ''wither-, withers. With'' has largely taken the place of AS. and ME. ''mid,'' with.]   '''1.''' Against: noting competition, opposition, or antagonism: as, to fight ''with'' the Romans (that is, against them); to vie ''with'' each other.
{{smaller block|For the most part wise and graue men doe naturally mislike ''with'' all sodaine innouations, specially of lawes.
{{right|''Puttenham,'' Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 86.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Sasquesahanocks, a mightie people, and mortall enemies ''with'' the Massawomeks.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, I. 182.}}}}
{{smaller block|The rival Moorish kings were waging civil war ''with'' each other in the vicinity of Granada.
{{right|''Irving,'' Granada, p. 83.}}}}

'''2.''' Noting association or connection. Particularly, expressing—(''a'') Proximity, accompaniment, companionship, or fellowship.
{{smaller block|They met at Ispahan (a Citie of Persia), and there Mahomet, falling ''with'' his horse, brake his neck.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 279.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Earl of Northumberland, being advertised thereof, came ''with'' a Power, assaulted the Castle, and after two Days Defence recovered it. {{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 137.}}}}
{{smaller block|The greatest News from Abroad is that the French King ''with'' his Cardinal are come again on this Side the Hills.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. v. 29.}}}}
{{smaller block|The globe goes round from west to east; and he must go round ''with'' it.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Gladstone on Church and State.}}}}
{{smaller block|Come and spend an evening ''with'' us.
{{right|''Dickens'', Cricket on the Hearth, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|There ''with'' her knights and dames was Guinevere.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Pelleas and Ettarre.}}}}
(''b'') Harmony, agreement, or alliance: as, one color may or may not go ''with'' another; to fight ''with'' the national troops; to side or vote ''with'' the reformers.
{{smaller block|He that is not ''with'' me is against me. {{right|Mat. xii. 30.}}}}
(''c'') Combination or composition: as, wine mixed ''with'' water. (''d'') Addition or conjunction: as, England (''with'' Wales), Scotland, and Ireland make the United Kingdom.
{{smaller block|Very wise, and ''with'' his wisdom very valiant.
{{right|''North'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 664, quoted in Abbot’s Shakesperian Grammar.}}}}
{{smaller block|Here were seen in profusion the orange, the citron, the fig, and pomegranate, ''with'' great plantations of mulberry trees, from which was produced the finest silk.
{{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 4.}}}}
(''e'') Communication, intercourse, or interaction.
<poem>''With'' thee she talks, ''with'' thee she moans,
''With'' thee she sighs, ''with'' thee she groans,
''With'' thee she says, “Farewell, mine own.”</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Surrey'', State of a Lover.}}}}
{{smaller block|I will buy ''with'' you, sell ''with'' you, talk ''with'' you, walk ''with'' you, and so following, but I will not eat ''with'' you, drink ''with'' you, nor pray ''with'' you. ''Shak.'', M. of V., i. 3. 36.
You have to do ''with'' other-guess-people now.
{{right|''Smollett'', Roderick Random, xlvii.}}}}

(''f'') Simultaneousness.
{{smaller block|''With'' every minute you do change a mind.
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., i. 1. 186.}}}}

'''3.''' As a property, attribute, or belonging of; in the possession, care, keeping, service, or employment of: as, to leave a package ''with'' one; to be ''with'' the A. B. Manufacturing Co.
{{smaller block|We may find Truth ''with'' one man as soon as in a Counsell.
{{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., i.}}}}

'''4.''' Having, possessing, bearing, or characterized by: as, the boy has come ''with'' the letter; Thebes, ''with'' its grand old walls; Rome, ''with'' her seven hills.
{{smaller block|<poem>A stately ship, . . .
''With'' all her bravery on.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', S. A., l. 717.}}}}
{{smaller block|His ministry was ''with'' much conviction and demonstration. ''N. Morton'', New England’s Memorial, p. 302.
There came into the shop a very learned man ''with'' an erect solemn air.
{{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 438.}}}}

'''5.''' In the region, sphere, or experience of; followed by a plural, among; also, in the sight, estimation, or opinion of: as, a holy prophet ''with'' God.
{{smaller block|<poem>The first of tho fre faithly was cald
Emynent the mighty, ''with'' men that hym knew.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 12442.}}}}

{{smaller block|''With'' men it is impossible, but not ''with'' God; for ''with'' God all things are possible.
{{right|Mat. x. 27.}}}}
{{smaller block|I had thought my life had borne more value ''with'' you.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Thierry and Theodoret, iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Those Antichthones, which are on the other side of the globe of the earth, are now out of the comfortable reach of the sunbeams, while it is day ''with'' us.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Sermons, xxxv.}}}}
{{smaller block|Such arguments had invincible force ''with'' those Pagan philosophers.
{{right|''Addison.''}}}}
{{smaller block|His integrity was perfect; it was a law of nature ''with'' him, rather than a choice or a principle.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 27.}}}}
'''6.''' In respect of; in relation to; as regards; as to: as, have patience ''with'' me; what is your will ''with'' me?
{{smaller block|<poem>How far am I grown
Behind-hand ''with'' fortune!</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Fair Maid of the Inn, iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|If we truely consider our Proceedings ''with'' the Spanyards and the rest, we haue no reason to despayre.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, I. 242.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thus will it ever be ''with'' him who trusts too much to woman.
{{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 217.}}}}
'''7.''' Like; analogously to; hence, specifically, at the same time or rate as; according to; in proportion to.
{{smaller block|<poem>As if ''with'' Circe she would change my shape.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., v. 3. 35.}}}}
{{smaller block|Their insolence and power increased ''with'' their number, and the seditions were also doubled ''with'' it.
{{right|''Swift'', Nobles and Commons, iii.}}}}
'''8.''' By. {{smaller|Indicating—(''a''†) An agent: as, slain ''with'' robbers.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Al thus ''with'' iewys I [Christ] am dyth.</poem>
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 247.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Ysiphile, betraysed ''with'' Jasoun.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 266.}}}}
{{smaller block|And so it was comaunded to be kept ''with'' x noble men; and thei were charged to take goode hede who com to assaien, and yef eny ther were that myght drawen out of the ston.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 100.}}}}
{{smaller block|He was torn to pieces ''with'' a bear.
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., v. 2. 68.}}}}
{{smaller block|At Flowers we were againe chased ''with'' foure French men of warre.
{{right|''Capt. John Smith'', Works, II. 209.}}}}
{{smaller block|He was sick and lame of the scurvy, so as he could but lie in the cabin-door, and give direction, and, it should seem, was badly assisted either ''with'' mate or mariners.
{{right|''N. Morton'', New England’s Memorial, p. 131.}}}}
(''b'') An instrument or means: as, to write ''with'' a pen; to cut ''with'' a knife; to heal ''with'' herbs.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thirle my soule ''with'' thi spere anoon.</poem>
{{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 26.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>You have paid me, equal heavens,
And sent my own rod to correct me ''with''.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|They had cut of his head upon y<sup>e</sup> cudy of his boat, had not y<sup>e</sup> man reskued him ''with'' a sword.
{{right|''Bradford'', Plymouth Plantation, p. 98.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And ''with'' faint Praises one another damn.</poem>
{{right|''Wycherley'', Plain Dealer, Prol.}}}}
(''c'') An accessory, as of material, contents, etc.: as, a ring set ''with'' diamonds; a ship laden ''with'' cotton; a bottle filled ''with'' water.
{{smaller block|Threescore carts laden ''with'' baggage.
{{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 23.}}}}
{{smaller block|The chiefe Citie, called St. Savadore, seated upon an exceeding high mountaine, 150. miles from the Sea, verie fertile, and inhabited ''with'' more than 100000. persons.
{{right|''Capt. John Smith'', Works, I. 49.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
